---
title: "Compiler Optimisation — Faster Without Changing the Answer"
description: "A rigorous introductory lesson with one small example, mathematical notation and a proof-oriented explanation."
---

## Start with an ordinary situation

A program computes (3 * 4) + (3 * 4). Can a compiler compute the multiplication only once?

## The core concept

Optimisation is justified only when transformed code preserves the source program's required observable behaviour.

## Express it mathematically

$$
\llbracket P\rrbracket(x)=\llbracket P'\rrbracket(x)
$$

**Every symbol explained:** P is the original program and P-prime is the transformed program; double brackets mean its externally observable result under input x. The equality is a simplified semantic-equivalence requirement for transformations.

**Substitute actual numbers:** For pure integer arithmetic with safe ranges, original: 3×4+3×4=24. Transform into t=3×4; result=t+t=24. The result stays equal while duplicated multiplication can be removed.

## Why it works

Common-subexpression elimination is safe for pure deterministic expressions when its language-specific semantics permit reuse. If the repeated expression calls a function with side effects, merging calls may change behaviour.

## Go one level deeper

Compiler optimisation often trades runtime speed, compilation time, code size and power. Proving equality on one input is not proof for all inputs.

## Common misunderstanding

Always distinguish a mathematical arithmetic identity from an identity that is valid for floats, integer overflow, concurrency or side-effectful code.

## Check your understanding

Explain the example with different numbers. Identify which assumption makes the derivation work, and which assumption would invalidate it. Then write the mathematical model again without looking.
